Hermann von Helmholtz

Hermann von Helmholtz (1821–1894) is, for the purposes of this book, the pivotal figure in the entire philosophical tradition. By measuring the speed of nerve impulses (and finding them surprisingly slow), he demonstrated that neural processing takes time—perception is not instantaneous contact with reality but the output of a process. He then proposed that perception is unconscious inference (unbewusster Schluss): the brain does not receive the world directly but infers the most likely external causes of its sensory signals, drawing on prior experience to resolve the inherent ambiguity of sensory data 1, 2. This is the direct ancestor of the Bayesian brain hypothesis, predictive processing, and the free energy principle. When Helmholtz wrote that “the sensations of the senses are tokens for our consciousness, it being left to our intelligence to learn how to comprehend their meaning,” he was describing the brain as a probabilistic inference engine.

Gustav Fechner

Gustav Fechner (1801–1887), in Elemente der Psychophysik 3, founded psychophysics by demonstrating that the relationship between physical stimulus intensity SS and perceived sensation PP follows a lawful mathematical function—the Weber–Fechner law: P=kln⁡(S/S0)P = k \ln(S/S_0). This was the first successful quantitative bridge between the physical world and the world model, establishing that the mapping from reality to representation is compressive and can be precisely characterized.

Franz Brentano

Franz Brentano (1838–1917) reintroduced intentionality as the defining characteristic of mental phenomena: every mental act (perceiving, believing, desiring, imagining) is directed at an object—it is about something 4. This “aboutness” is what any neural theory of world modeling must ultimately explain: how do patterns of electrochemical activity come to be about objects, events, and states of affairs in the external world? Brentano’s question has never gone away.

William James

William James (1842–1910) produced the most influential English-language psychology of the 19th century 5. Consciousness is not a chain of discrete ideas but a continuous stream—a dynamic, contextually rich flow. Neural habit is the physiological substrate of cognition: well-worn pathways of activity that free higher processes for novel situations. The James–Lange theory of emotion—that we are afraid because we run, not the reverse—casts emotion as the perception of the body’s own physiological response, a form of interoceptive inference that modern predictive processing has embraced.

Ernst Mach

Ernst Mach (1838–1916) argued in The Analysis of Sensations 6 that science should abandon the metaphysical distinction between “physical” and “mental” and deal only with elements (sensations) and the functional relations among them. The task of any good model, whether scientific or cognitive, is to describe regularities among elements with maximal economy of thought (Denkökonomie). This principle of descriptive parsimony is a qualitative forerunner of the variational free energy principle’s mandate to minimize model complexity.

Wilhelm Wundt

Wilhelm Wundt (1832–1920) founded the first formal laboratory of experimental psychology in Leipzig in 1879, marking the institutional separation of psychology from philosophy 7. His method of trained experimental introspection—in which observers reported the elementary components of conscious experience under rigorously controlled stimulus conditions—was an attempt to decompose the world model into its basic constituents through systematic observation. Central to Wundt’s theory was apperception: the active, volitional process by which the mind synthesizes disparate sensory elements into a unified, attended experience. This concept—attention as an active, selective, integrative process that shapes what enters consciousness—anticipates the role of precision-weighting and attentional gain modulation in predictive processing, where not all prediction errors are treated equally, and the mind must actively select and weight its inputs.

Charles Sanders Peirce

Charles Sanders Peirce (1839–1914) introduced abduction—inference to the best explanation—as a third fundamental mode of reasoning alongside deduction and induction 8, 9, 10. Where deduction unfolds consequences from premises and induction generalizes from observed instances, abduction generates hypotheses that would, if true, explain the data at hand. This is precisely the inferential move that Helmholtz attributed to unconscious perception—-and that the Bayesian brain formalizes as posterior inference over a generative model. Peirce’s broader semiotics (theory of signs) provides an additional philosophical resource: neural states can be understood as signs of their external causes, related to those causes through interpretants (further neural states that specify how the sign is to be read), producing an inferential cascade with no foundational, uninterpreted terminus—representations all the way down.
